questions.topic: The interval content of a motive
questions.learningObjective: state what a motive is and identify the intervals inside it
questions.stem: A melody in c major opens with three notes: g4 as a quarter note, b4 as a quarter note and c5 as a quarter note. What makes this a motive rather than merely three notes, and what is its interval content?

options.text: It is a motive because it is a short figure of a recognisable shape, and its interval content is a major third from g4 to b4 followed by a minor second from b4 to c5
It is a motive because all three notes belong to the c major scale, and its interval content is an octave from g4 to c5 taken as a whole
options.misconception: treats scale membership as the definition of a motive

options.text: It is a motive because it is three notes long, and its interval content is a minor third from g4 to b4 followed by a major second
options.misconception: believes the figure's length defines a motive and misreads both intervals

options.text: It is a motive because it begins the piece, and its interval content is the two semitones by which the figure rises overall
options.misconception: takes a rising figure's total motion as a single interval

questions.explanation: A motive is a short figure that a composer treats as a unit and expects to be heard again, and being at the start of a piece is not what makes one. The defining feature is that the figure has a shape a listener can recognise, which means its intervals matter as much as its pitches. Here there are two intervals and both are doing work: g4 to b4 is four semitones, a major third, and b4 to c5 is one semitone, a minor second. A leap followed by a step is a common shape for an opening motive because the leap establishes a register and direction and the step then turns, so the figure is stable enough to be recognisable but not so smooth that it disappears into the scale. The trap in the third option is the useful one to check, since reading the major third as minor and the minor second as major would give an entirely different shape and one that is not in this figure at all.
questions.hint: Measure the two gaps between the three notes, and ask whether the figure could be recognised again in another key.

questions.topic: The span of a stated motive
questions.learningObjective: compute the total span of a three-note motive
questions.stem: A motive is written g4 quarter note, b4 quarter note and c5 quarter note. Counting semitones from the first note to the last, how wide is the figure's total span?
questions.explanation: Up from g4, g-sharp is one, a two, a-sharp three, b four and c five, so g4 to c5 is five semitones. The second route adds the two steps of the figure: g4 up to b4 is four semitones, b4 up to c5 is one, and four plus one is five. The third route names it, since g to c spans the letter names g, a, b, c, which is a fourth, and a perfect fourth is five semitones. Five semitones is a fourth rather than an octave, which matters because a motive that spans a fourth can be inverted to one that spans a fifth or a sixth and will still fit comfortably in a melody, whereas a motive spanning an octave would double in span when inverted. The trap is twelve, which would be the span if the figure ended an octave above where it began.
questions.hint: Count the two steps separately and add them, then check by naming the interval from the outer notes.

questions.topic: Inverting a motive and what changes
questions.learningObjective: describe how inversion alters a motive's intervals
questions.stem: A motive rises from g4 by a major third to b4 and then rises a minor second to c5. Its inversion turns the same figure upside down. What happens to the two intervals, and why is the result still recognisably the same motive?

options.text: Each interval is replaced by the distance from itself to an octave, so the major third of four semitones becomes eight and the minor second of one becomes eleven, and the figure remains recognisable because the order of its turns is preserved
Each interval keeps its size and only its direction reverses, so the figure rises by a minor second and then falls by a major third
options.misconception: believes inversion reverses direction without altering interval size

options.text: Each interval is doubled, so the major third becomes a major sixth and the minor second becomes a minor third, and the figure is recognisable only because the rhythm is unchanged
options.misconception: describes augmentation as the effect of inversion

options.text: The intervals are replaced by their complements to a perfect fifth, so the major third becomes a minor second and the minor second becomes a major third
options.misconception: takes the complement to a fifth rather than to an octave

questions.explanation: Inversion is a reflection about a horizontal line, and reflecting a figure about a line turns each interval into the distance that completes an octave with it. A major third of four semitones therefore becomes eight, a minor sixth, and a minor second of one becomes eleven, a major seventh. The shape is changed, and a listener hearing only the inversion would not place it in the same key, which is the composer's usual reason for using it. What makes it still the same motive is that the rhythm is untouched and the order of the figure's turns is reversed, so the same skeleton is heard. The trap in the second option is that a major third and a minor second are not complements of each other, since four plus one is five, not an octave. The trap in the third option describes augmentation, which changes durations and not pitches, and the trap in the fourth option uses a perfect fifth as the reference when inversion is defined by the octave.
questions.hint: Reflecting a figure about a line replaces each gap with what completes an octave with it.

questions.topic: The interval produced by inverting a third
questions.learningObjective: compute the interval that inverts a stated third
questions.stem: A motive contains a major third of four semitones between its first and second notes. The motive is inverted, and each interval is replaced by the distance that completes an octave with it. Counting semitones, how wide is the interval between the inverted first and second notes?
questions.explanation: An octave is twelve semitones, and the distance that completes an octave with a four-semitone interval is twelve less four, which is eight. The second route names the interval: a third inverted about a fixed line becomes a sixth, because the two notes now sit on opposite sides of the axis, and a sixth of eight semitones is a minor sixth. The third route is to check against the original's quality, since a major third inverts to a minor sixth and major thirds are four semitones while minor sixths are eight. Eight semitones is also a large interval to sing, which is one practical reason composers invert a motive and then place it an octave lower than it first appeared, so that the inverted figure fits the vocal or instrumental range. The trap is four, which is the size of the original interval, and four is what a listener would measure if the inversion were actually a transposition.
questions.hint: Take twelve semitones and subtract the size of the original interval.

questions.topic: A retrograde and what it does to a figure
questions.learningObjective: describe how a retrograde alters a figure's direction while keeping its rhythm
questions.stem: A motive runs c4 quarter, e4 quarter, g4 quarter, b4 quarter, a4 quarter and g4 quarter, rising three times and falling twice. Its retrograde plays the six notes in the opposite order with the same note values. What changes, and what stays?

options.text: The direction of every interval is reversed, so the figure that rose three times and fell twice now rises twice and falls three times, while the note values stay in the same order from the end backwards
Only the first and last notes are exchanged, so the middle of the figure is unchanged and the number of rising steps stays at three
options.misconception: believes a retrograde swaps the outer notes only

options.text: The intervals are reversed but the rhythm is also reversed, so a figure of quarters and halves becomes a figure of halves and quarters
options.misconception: believes a retrograde turns the rhythm back to front as well

options.text: The figure is unchanged apart from its key, since a retrograde is the same as playing the tune in another key
options.misconception: confuses a retrograde with a transposition

questions.explanation: A retrograde takes a figure and plays it backwards, and the consequence for the shape is exact. The three rising steps of the original become three falling steps, and the two falling steps become two rising steps, so the retrograde rises twice and falls three times. What does not change is the note values, and this is the part that is easy to get wrong. If the motive were three quarters, a half and two quarters, the retrograde is that same sequence of values starting at the end of the figure, so the first note of the retrograde is a quarter and the second is a half. The rhythm is reversed in the sense that it runs from the end to the beginning, but the values themselves are not rescaled or re-emphasised. The consequence for a composer is that a retrograde is easy to recognise and hard to disguise, since the ear catches the rhythm first, so it is usually used where recognition is wanted. The second trap describes a palindrome, which is a special property only some figures have.
questions.hint: Reverse the order of the intervals and leave the note values alone, then count the new rises.

questions.topic: The rising steps a retrograde produces
questions.learningObjective: count the rising steps in the retrograde of a stated motive
questions.stem: A motive is written c4 quarter, e4 quarter, g4 quarter, b4 quarter, a4 quarter and g4 quarter. How many rising steps does the motive's retrograde contain, when the retrograde is the same six notes played in reverse order?
questions.explanation: Read the motive forwards and the gaps are three rises, from c4 to e4, e4 to g4 and g4 to b4, followed by two falls, from b4 to a4 and a4 to g4. The retrograde plays g4, a4, b4, g4, e4, c4, and reading those backwards gives two rises, g4 to a4 and a4 to b4, and three falls. The second route is a general rule rather than a count: reversing a sequence turns every rise into a fall and every fall into a rise, so the number of rises in the retrograde must equal the number of falls in the original, which is two. Two is also worth stating as a property rather than a coincidence, since the same argument shows the retrograde's total span is unchanged and its highest note becomes its first. The trap is three, which is the number of rising steps in the original and is what a listener who has not reversed the figure properly would report.
questions.hint: Reverse the six notes and count the rises, or note that a retrograde swaps rises for falls.

questions.topic: Augmenting a motive
questions.learningObjective: describe augmentation and why a composer uses it
questions.stem: A composer takes a motive of three notes and rewrites it so that every note value is doubled, a quarter becoming a half and an eighth becoming a quarter, while the pitches stay the same. What is this transformation called and what does it do to the character of the figure?

options.text: It is augmentation, and doubling every value makes the figure sound broader and more heavily weighted, so the same idea arrives more slowly and with more weight behind it
It is augmentation, and doubling every value makes the figure sound quicker because twice as many notes of the same length must fit into the same time
options.misconception: confuses lengthening with the effect of adding notes

options.text: It is inversion, because reversing the direction of a figure requires each of its values to be lengthened to keep the total span the same
options.misconception: calls augmentation inversion

options.text: It is fragmentation, because splitting a figure into shorter pieces necessarily shortens each of the pieces that remain
options.misconception: calls augmentation fragmentation

questions.explanation: Augmentation changes only one thing, the durations, and the definition is that each note value is multiplied by the same factor, so the proportions between the notes are preserved exactly while the whole figure is stretched. The character changes with it. A motive in short values sounds agile and nervous, and the same motive in doubled values sounds broader and more declarative, because the ear reads a longer note as more emphatic and a shorter one as more urgent. This is why augmentation is the standard way to present a subject's counterpart in a slow movement: a fugue subject that is too quick to be sung as a counterline can be augmented so that it fits the pace of the accompanying voice. The trap in the second option gets the arithmetic backwards, since doubling every value means the figure takes twice as long rather than fitting into the same time. The remaining two traps name other transformations, and both of those change the pitch content rather than the durations.
questions.hint: Ask which single feature of the figure has been multiplied, and check that its proportions are unchanged.

questions.topic: The new length of an augmented motive
questions.learningObjective: compute the length of a motive after augmentation
questions.stem: A motive has a total length of six eighth notes. It is augmented so that every note value is doubled. Measured in quarter notes, what is the new total length of the figure?
questions.explanation: Six eighth notes are three quarter notes, since a quarter note is two eighth notes and three pairs of eighths make three quarters. Doubling every value doubles the total, so the augmented figure is six quarter notes long. The second route works in eighths throughout: doubling six eighths gives twelve eighths, and twelve eighths are six quarters, which is the same figure as three half notes, since a half note is four eighths. The reason this matters musically is that augmentation preserves the proportions between the notes, so a motive of two eighths and a quarter is still in that ratio afterwards, and only the overall scale has changed. The trap is three, which is the original length in quarter notes, or twelve, which is the original length counted in the new values' unit rather than in quarters.
questions.hint: Convert the original length to quarter notes first, then double it once.

questions.topic: Fragmenting a motive
questions.learningObjective: describe how a fragment of a motive preserves or loses its identity
questions.stem: A composer takes the first three of a motive's four notes and uses only those three, in order, at several different pitches, leaving the fourth note out entirely. What has been done to the motive, and what is the risk?

options.text: The motive has been fragmented, and the risk is that three notes carry less information than four, so a listener may stop hearing the connection to the whole figure
The motive has been fragmented, and the risk is that dropping a note makes the figure irregular in a way that a singer cannot execute at speed
options.misconception: treats an irregular figure as a vocal problem

options.text: The motive has been inverted, because using only part of a figure inverts the part that is left
options.misconception: calls fragmentation inversion

options.text: The motive has been augmented, because using fewer notes at the same length values necessarily makes each note longer in performance
options.misconception: calls fragmentation augmentation

questions.explanation: Fragmentation is the technique of taking a recognisable piece of a longer figure and using that piece on its own, usually repeated at different pitches so that the music appears to be working from a smaller cell. The risk is exactly the one the option names and it is a matter of information. A four-note motive has more distinguishing content than a three-note one, because there are more possible arrangements of three notes than of two, so a short fragment is correspondingly harder for a listener to identify. This is why composers tend to keep the most characteristic part: if the fourth note of a motive carried the distinctive leap, then dropping it and keeping the first three removes the very thing that made the motive recognisable. The transformation is also the engine of motivic development, since a fragment repeated at rising pitches produces a sequence of the figure's own material, and a fragment repeated in a new rhythm produces a new melody built from the old one.
questions.hint: Ask how many notes were discarded and how much identifying content the figure had to begin with.

questions.topic: The fraction of a motive a fragment keeps
questions.learningObjective: compute the proportion of a motive retained by a fragment
questions.stem: A motive contains four notes. A fragment keeps the first three of them in the same order and at the same pitches, and discards the fourth. What fraction of the motive's notes does the fragment contain?
questions.explanation: Three of the four notes survive, and three divided by four is three quarters, which is zero point seven five. The second route is to compute the complement: the fragment discards one of four notes, and one quarter of the motive is gone, so what remains is one less one quarter, which is three quarters. The third route is to check against a doubled figure, since three quarters of four is three and three quarters of eight is six, and the relationship between the fragment and the whole is the same in both cases because a fraction does not depend on the size of the thing measured. Musically, three quarters is worth naming because fragmentation rarely removes exactly a quarter, and a fragment of two thirds of a motive or one half of it is just as common; what matters is that the composer has kept enough of the figure for recognition, and three notes out of four is usually enough while two out of four often is not.
questions.hint: Divide the number of notes kept by the number in the whole motive.

questions.topic: What a developing variation preserves
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a developing variation from a decorative one
questions.stem: A variation presents the theme's melodic shape but replaces its ornamentation, stretches its note values, and alters its intervals so that the outline is no longer literal. Its harmony, however, follows the theme's harmonic plan closely. What makes this a developing variation rather than a decorative one?

options.text: It is developing because the variation keeps the theme's harmonic plan and its essential character while changing how the melody is built, so the music grows out of the theme instead of merely looking like it
It is developing because the theme's melody has been altered, and any alteration of a theme's melody counts as development of the material
options.misconception: treats any change to the melody as development

options.text: It is developing because the variation is longer than the theme, and length is what allows a variation to develop the material it presents
options.misconception: judges development by the length of the variation

options.text: It is developing because it appears before the recapitulation, and a variation placed early in a movement is by definition a developing one
options.misconception: judges development by where the variation sits in the form

questions.explanation: The distinction is between a variation that keeps the theme's identity and one that only keeps its surface. A developing variation preserves the things that make the theme the theme, above all its harmonic plan and its general character, and then works on the melody itself, altering intervals, changing rhythms and redistributing the notes. Because the harmony follows the theme, a listener can hear the connection even at the point where the melodic outline has been obscured, and that is what makes the variation developmental: the music is still thinking the theme's thoughts. A decorative variation does the opposite, keeping the melody note for note and adding surface interest above and around it, and the two may sit side by side in the same set. The trap in the second option is the one worth watching, since a decorative variation also alters the melody, by ornamenting it, and the difference is what is left when the surface is stripped away. Position in the movement and the length of the variation have nothing to do with the classification.
questions.hint: Ask what is preserved when the melody's surface is removed.

questions.topic: The length of a stretched variation
questions.learningObjective: compute the length of a variation whose values are doubled
questions.stem: A theme is sixteen bars long, and in one of its variations the composer keeps the theme's harmonic rhythm but doubles every melodic value, so that the melody is stretched to twice its original length. How many bars does that variation run?
questions.explanation: The theme is sixteen bars and every melodic value is doubled, so the melody now occupies twice the time it did, which is thirty-two bars. The second route follows the harmonic rhythm, which is stated to be preserved: if the harmony still changes at the same rate, then the doubled melody is filling twice as many notes into each harmonic unit, and sixteen bars of harmony now has to accommodate thirty-two bars of melody, so the natural reading is that the variation runs to thirty-two bars. This is exactly what a developing variation does to slow music: the harmony is kept as a set of pillars at their original spacing while the line above stretches across twice the distance, and the gap between the pillars is what the melody has to fill. The trap is sixteen, which is the length of the theme, and eight, which would be the case if the values were halved.
questions.hint: Multiply the theme's length by the factor applied to the melody.

questions.topic: The ritornello principle
questions.learningObjective: state what a ritornello is and why it returns
questions.stem: In a movement for solo instrument and orchestra, a long instrumental passage appears between shorter sections for the soloist. It returns several times, each time in a different key. What is this passage and why does it return?

options.text: It is the ritornello, a self-contained instrumental refrain that returns after each solo section, and it returns because its return is the signal that the solo is over and that the orchestra is taking the music back
It is the ritornello, and it returns because the soloist has used up all the material available to them and the orchestra must resume the argument
options.misconception: makes a formal signal into an exhaustion of material

options.text: It is the da capo of the solo part, and it returns because the soloist is instructed by the score to play the same passage again an octave lower
options.misconception: confuses the instrumental refrain with a repeat instruction for the soloist

options.text: It is the coda, and it returns because a coda is by definition the last section and is therefore played more than once
options.misconception: treats the coda as a repeating section

questions.explanation: A ritornello is a self-contained passage for the full orchestra that frames the solo sections, and its defining feature is that it returns, transposed as necessary to a new key each time. The return is the compositional signal, and that is what makes the form readable. A listener who has heard the ritornello three times can hear a soloist's entry as an answer to it and the ritornello's re-entry as a closing, and the whole alternation acquires a shape that neither the solo nor the orchestra would have alone. Because the ritornello returns in a different key, it also carries the tonal argument: the soloist's excursions are measured by how far the music has moved away from where the orchestra left it, and the reappearance in a new key registers as a new stage of that journey. The trap in the second option mistakes a formal signal for a shortage of material, and the fourth is confused about the coda, which is a closing section and appears once.
questions.hint: Ask what the returning passage is for, and what its re-entry tells a listener about the solo sections.

questions.topic: How much music a ritornello contributes
questions.learningObjective: total the duration of a ritornello across its returns
questions.stem: A movement's ritornello is twenty-four bars long and it returns five times in the movement. Measured in bars, how much of the movement is taken up by the ritornello altogether?
questions.explanation: Five returns of twenty-four bars give a hundred and twenty bars. The second route is to total one return at a time, which is twenty-four, and then add twenty-four five times, which is twenty-four plus twenty-four plus twenty-four plus twenty-four plus twenty-four. The third route is to note that five returns is two more than three, and three returns would be seventy-two, so five is seventy-two plus forty-eight, which is a hundred and twenty. The reason the figure is worth computing is that it measures the proportion of the movement the frame occupies, and in the works where the soloist's material is a small part of the whole, the ritornello is the larger share, which tells a listener before hearing a note that the orchestra is the principal character. The trap is forty-eight, which is the total for two returns rather than five, or twenty-four, which counts one return and forgets the first.
questions.hint: Multiply the length of one return by the number of returns, and check by adding one at a time.

questions.topic: Why a fugue subject needs a tonal answer
questions.learningObjective: explain what a tonal answer adjusts and why the adjustment is necessary
questions.stem: A fugue subject begins on the tonic and leaps a fifth upward. When the answer enters a fifth below, that leap would become a fourth above the new starting note, and a fourth in that position is a dissonance. What has the composer done about it?

options.text: The answer is made tonal: the interval is widened so that it becomes a fifth again, the figure is adjusted to stay inside the new key, and the entry is still heard as the same subject
The answer is made real: the subject is transposed down a fifth with every interval unchanged, and the dissonance is left in because dissonance is what a fugue is for
options.misconception: leaves the dissonance in place and mistakes it for the point of the technique

options.text: The answer is made tonal: the subject is transposed down a fifth and then inverted, so that the fifth becomes a sixth and no dissonance arises
options.misconception: reaches the right answer by describing an inversion rather than an adjustment

options.text: The answer is made real: the subject is transposed down a fifth and the offending note is omitted from the answer, so the figure is shorter in the second voice
options.misconception: believes a real answer drops a note from the subject

questions.explanation: This is the whole reason two kinds of fugue answer exist. A real answer is a literal transposition down a fifth with every interval untouched, and it works only when the subject's shape survives the move. A leap of a fifth from the tonic, transposed down a fifth, becomes a leap of a fourth, and a fourth measured upward from the dominant is the interval between two notes a tritone apart once the octave is taken into account, which is a dissonance in the second voice against a first voice that has not moved. The tonal answer solves this by adjusting the interval, widening the fourth to a fifth, and by adjusting the rest of the figure so that every note stays inside the new key. The entry is then heard as the same subject because the rhythm and the general shape survive, and the ear accepts the changed intervals as a reinterpretation rather than as a mistake. This is also why tonal answers sound more integrated and real answers sound more like a second voice stating the tune again.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a fifth when the whole figure is moved down a fifth, and whether a fourth in that position is stable.

questions.topic: The first note of a tonal answer
questions.learningObjective: compute the pitch at which a tonal answer begins
questions.stem: A fugue subject in c major begins on c5. In the scheme where c4 is numbered sixty, c5 is numbered seventy-two. The tonal answer begins a perfect fourth lower, which is five semitones. What number is the answer's first note?
questions.explanation: A perfect fourth is five semitones, so subtracting five from seventy-two gives sixty-seven. The second route names the note as well as numbering it, and the name is a useful check: counting up from sixty-seven gives sixty-eight, sixty-nine, seventy, seventy-one and seventy-two, so sixty-seven is the note five semitones below c5, which is g4. The third route is to use the transposition rule directly, since a real or tonal answer begins a fifth below the subject, and a fifth below c5 is g4, and g4 is numbered sixty-seven because g is seven semitones above c and c4 is sixty. All three routes agree, which is the point of running them, since the arithmetic is easy to get wrong in the direction of the subtraction. Sixty-seven is also the number that makes the interval from the answer's first note to the subject's first note a perfect fourth, which is the adjustment that makes the entry tonal.
questions.hint: Subtract the number of semitones from the starting number, and name the note to confirm it.

questions.topic: What makes a double fugue double
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a double fugue from a fugue with a second subject
questions.stem: A fugue begins with a subject of six bars, and a second theme of three bars is then stated as a counter-subject before any of the first theme is answered. Later the two themes combine in the same voice. What makes this a double fugue?

options.text: It is a double fugue because two subjects of comparable independence are each developed throughout the movement and are finally combined, so that neither functions only as an accompaniment to the other
It is a double fugue because two subjects are present at the start, so the number of themes at the beginning is what decides the category
options.misconception: counts the themes introduced rather than testing their independence

options.text: It is a double fugue because the second subject is shorter than the first, so the two subjects are of unequal length and inequality is the criterion
options.misconception: judges a double fugue by the relative lengths of its subjects

options.text: It is a double fugue because the two themes are combined in one voice, and a combination is only possible in a fugue with more than one subject
options.misconception: makes the combination the definition rather than a consequence of independence

questions.explanation: The word double points at the treatment, not at the count. In a single fugue the exposition states the subject and answers it, and any counter-subject is subordinate, appearing in the spaces between entries and never taking over. In a double fugue there are two subjects of comparable weight, each is answered in turn, and each continues to be developed after the other has been introduced, so that the movement ends by combining them. That is why the second subject in this example is stated before the first is answered: the delay in the answer is itself a sign that the first theme is not the only voice of the argument. The practical test is what happens to each theme later. A subject that is only ever heard with the other one is a counter-subject, and a passage in which the two themes are combined in a single voice, which is the hardest thing to write and the moment a double fugue is judged to have succeeded, is not something a single-subject fugue can produce at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether each theme is developed in its own right after the other has been introduced.

questions.topic: The subject material of a double fugue
questions.learningObjective: total the subject material stated in every section of a double fugue
questions.stem: A double fugue has one subject of seven bars and another of three bars, and the movement has two sections. Each subject is stated once in each section, with no repeats and no shortening. How many bars of subject material does the movement contain?
questions.explanation: One section contains seven bars of the first subject and three of the second, which is ten bars, and two sections of ten bars give twenty. The second route is to count subjects rather than sections, since there are two subjects each stated twice, giving four statements, and the two long ones contribute seven bars each and the two short ones three each, so seven plus seven plus three plus three is twenty. The reason the arithmetic is worth doing is that it shows how much of the movement is thematic rather than connective, and a double fugue in which the twenty bars of subject occupy only a small part of the whole is a piece whose real substance lies in the episodes between the statements. The trap is fourteen, which counts only the first subject across both sections, or ten, which is the content of one section rather than of the movement.
questions.hint: Add the two subject lengths for one section, then multiply by the number of sections.

questions.topic: A round and its entry interval
questions.learningObjective: state how a round differs from a canon and what fixes its entry interval
questions.stem: Four singers perform the same eight-bar tune, the second beginning as soon as the first reaches the end of its first two bars, and so on for each voice. What is this texture, and what fixes the interval at which the voices enter?

options.text: It is a round, a canon in which every voice sings the same tune from the same note, and the entry interval is fixed by how much of the tune each voice sings before the next one joins, here two bars
It is a round, and the entry interval is fixed by the key of the tune, so each voice must enter at the point where the tune next reaches the tonic
options.misconception: claims the key fixes the entry interval

options.text: It is a canon at the octave, and the entry interval is fixed by the length of the tune, so each voice waits until the previous one has finished
options.misconception: describes a canon rather than a round and misidentifies the interval

options.text: It is a round, and the entry interval is fixed by the number of voices, since four voices require each to enter a quarter of the way through
options.misconception: claims the voice count fixes the entry interval

questions.explanation: A round is the simplest kind of canon and it has two defining features that are worth stating separately. All the voices sing the same tune, and they all begin at the same pitch, which is what distinguishes a round from the general family of canons, where voices may start at different pitches and even sing a different melody. The second feature is that the entry points are equally spaced, so the piece divides into repeating units of a fixed length, and that unit is the entry interval. Here each voice begins two bars after the one before, so the repeating unit is two bars, and the eight-bar tune is heard four times over before the pattern closes. This is why rounds are so often used as a first exercise in counterpoint: the composer's problem is reduced to writing one tune and then checking that it can be superimposed on itself at the chosen interval without producing unacceptable intervals against itself.
questions.hint: Ask whether all the voices start at the same pitch, and then count the bars between one entry and the next.

questions.topic: The gap between the first and last entries of a round
questions.learningObjective: compute the gap between the first and last entries of a round
questions.stem: A round for four voices has an eight-bar tune, and each voice enters two bars after the voice before it. How many bars elapse between the first voice's entry and the last voice's entry?
questions.explanation: There are three gaps between four voices, not four, and each gap is two bars, so three times two is six bars. The second route is to name the bars: the first voice enters at bar one, the second at bar three, the third at bar five and the fourth at bar seven, and the difference between bar one and bar seven is six. The third route checks the pattern: the entry points are one, three, five and seven, which are evenly spaced by two, and the last of them is six bars after the first. Six is also the number that matters musically, because it tells a singer how much of the tune has already been sung when the last voice arrives: the first voice has completed six of the eight bars, so only two bars of the tune remain before the pattern begins again. The trap is eight, which is the length of the tune, and four, which counts the voices instead of the gaps between them.
questions.hint: Count the gaps between the entries, which is one fewer than the number of voices.

questions.topic: The degrees a blues progression varies
questions.learningObjective: identify which scale degrees a blues progression alters and why
questions.stem: A twelve-bar blues in a uses the chords i, i, i, i, iv, iv, i, v, iv, iv, i and v, and the tonic chord of bar seven is sometimes played as a dominant seventh rather than as a plain tonic triad. Which degrees are free to vary, and what does the variation do?

options.text: The fourth and the fifth degrees are the variable ones, and adding a seventh to the tonic turns the subdominant's natural stillness into a dominant pull, so that bar seven leads onward instead of standing still
The first and the third degrees are the variable ones, and altering them changes the colour of the opening without affecting the pull towards the close
options.misconception: claims the opening chords are the variable ones

options.text: The second and the sixth degrees are the variable ones, and the blues form never uses them at all, so there is nothing there to vary
options.misconception: names degrees the form does not use as its variable ones

options.text: No degree is variable, because a blues progression is a fixed sequence of chords and any change to it destroys the form
options.misconception: believes the progression is fixed against any variation

questions.explanation: The chords that a blues form allows to vary are the two that are not the tonic, the subdominant and the dominant, and the reason is structural rather than decorative. The tonic fills half of the twelve bars and the form depends on it being unchanging, so altering the first degree would undermine what the pattern is for. The fourth degree, which is a minor subdominant borrowed from the parallel minor, and the fifth degree are the harmonic joints of the form, and both are freely altered: the tonic at bar seven may be given a seventh so that it pulls towards the dominant at bar eight instead of resting, and the dominant may take a ninth or be extended in other ways. The result is a form that is recognisable from a bare skeleton and yet different on every chorus, and the variation is what lets a blues sit under a singer for many choruses without becoming static.
questions.hint: Ask which chords the form depends on staying the same, and which act as its joints.

questions.topic: Counting the tonic bars of a blues
questions.learningObjective: count how many bars of a blues progression carry the tonic
questions.stem: A twelve-bar blues in a uses the pattern i, i, i, i, iv, iv, i, v, iv, iv, i and v, one chord per bar. How many of the twelve bars carry the tonic chord?
questions.explanation: Read down the list of twelve and count the i's: bars one, two, three, four, seven and eleven, which is six bars. The second route is to count the other two chords and subtract, since the subdominant appears at bars five, six, eight and nine, which is four bars, and the dominant appears at bars ten and twelve, which is two bars, so twelve less four less two leaves six. The reason the proportion is worth knowing is that a blues in which the tonic occupies half the form is a form built on a very stable ground, and the four subdominant bars and two dominant bars are the only points at which the harmony does anything, which is precisely why those are the bars a soloist uses to move and the bars a variation most often alters. The trap is four, which counts the first four bars and stops, and four is also the number of subdominant bars, so it is an easy double error.
questions.hint: Count the tonic bars directly, or subtract the other two chords from twelve.

questions.topic: The flattened third of a blues scale
questions.learningObjective: compute the interval from a tonic to the flattened third of a blues scale
questions.stem: A blues in a uses the scale a, c, d, e-flat, e, f and g, in which the third degree of the major scale is lowered. Counting semitones from a4 up to c5, how wide is the interval from the tonic to that flattened third?
questions.explanation: Up from a4, a-sharp is one, b two and c three, so a4 to c5 is three semitones, a minor third. The second route is to name it: a to c spans the letter names a, b, c, which is a third, and a third of three semitones is a minor third. The third route is to start from the major third and widen it, since a to c-sharp is four semitones and lowering the upper note by a semitone leaves three. Three is the interval that gives the blues scale its name and its sound, because the minor third against the major seventh of the same scale is the clash that makes the scale recognisable; a scale with a major third instead would be the ordinary major scale and would have no blues character at all. The trap is four, which is the major third before it was flattened, and the trap of two, which is the interval from a to the b that lies between them.
questions.hint: Count up a semitone at a time, and check the interval name from the two letter names.

questions.topic: The stride left hand
questions.learningObjective: describe the stride left hand and the beat it occupies
questions.stem: A pianist's left hand plays a single low note on the first beat of each bar and a chord higher up on the second, then repeats the alternation on the third and fourth beats. What is this figure called, and what does it do to the music?

options.text: It is the stride left hand, and because the bass and the chord alternate on every beat it both outlines the harmony and keeps the pulse driving, which is why it can carry a tune in the right hand for many bars
It is the stride left hand, and because it plays two notes on every beat it fills the bass register so densely that the right hand has nothing left to do
options.misconception: believes a dense left hand leaves the right hand idle

options.text: It is a walking bass, and because it alternates a single note and a chord it is the same figure played by a double bass instead of a piano
options.misconception: confuses the stride left hand with a walking bass

options.text: It is an Alberti bass, and because the low note and the chord alternate it is a broken-chord pattern in the left hand of the piano
options.misconception: confuses the stride left hand with a broken-chord figure

questions.explanation: The stride figure is defined by the alternation of a bass note and a chord on every beat, so two events occupy each beat and the hand moves a long way between them. Because the bass note names the root of the harmony and the chord supplies the rest, the left hand alone conveys the full harmonic content of the bar, and because the alternation is on every beat rather than every half bar, the pulse never stops. That combination is what makes stride so effective under a melody: the harmony is complete and the beat is unbroken, so the right hand is freed to carry a tune and the ear is given constant rhythmic information. The walking bass is a different figure, a single line of quarter notes moving by step through the chord tones, and the Alberti figure is a broken chord in a repeated low-high-middle-high pattern. Neither alternates a single bass note with a chord in the way the stride does.
questions.hint: Ask how many events occupy each beat and what two different kinds of information the left hand supplies.

questions.topic: How long a bar lasts in a stride piano passage
questions.learningObjective: convert a bar's beat count into seconds at a stated tempo
questions.stem: A stride piano passage is in common time at a tempo of 160 quarter notes to the minute, and the left hand plays a bass note and then a chord on each of the four beats. How many seconds does one bar last?
questions.explanation: Common time has four quarter notes to the bar, and at 160 to the minute a quarter note lasts sixty over one hundred and sixty of a second, which is three eighths of a second, so four beats take four times three eighths, which is a second and a half. The second route is to work in minutes: four quarter notes at one hundred and sixty to the minute is four over one hundred and sixty of a minute, and multiplying by sixty gives one and a half seconds exactly. The stride detail is worth keeping in view, because the two left-hand events per beat mean there are eight attacks in the bar, so the passage carries eight evenly spaced impulses spread across one and a half seconds. The trap is four, which is the count of beats rather than the time they take, and the trap of three eighths of a second, which is the length of a single beat and would answer a different question.
questions.hint: Multiply the beats in the bar by the length of one beat, which is sixty divided by the tempo.

questions.topic: The defining property of a walking bass
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a bass line a walking bass
questions.stem: A bass player plays one note on every beat, moving from chord tone to chord tone by step and filling the gaps with notes that belong to the chord. What makes this a walking bass rather than any other moving bass line?

options.text: It plays a continuous quarter-note line that fills each beat without rests, moving smoothly through the chord tones, so that the line connects one harmony to the next instead of punctuating them
It plays a continuous quarter-note line that fills each beat, and it must use only the root of each chord, since the other chord members are the pianist's business
options.misconception: restricts a walking bass to root notes only

options.text: It plays a line that leaps from the root of one chord to the root of the next, since a walking line is defined by its leaps rather than by its rhythm
options.misconception: defines a walking bass by leaps rather than by its rhythm

options.text: It plays the same figure at the same speed under every chord, so that the line is a fixed pattern rather than a response to the harmony
options.misconception: makes a walking bass a fixed repeated figure

questions.explanation: The name describes the motion: the line walks, one note per beat, in even quarter notes with no rests and no held notes, and it travels through the chord tones of the harmony currently sounding so that each beat is consonant with what the other players are doing. Because the line is continuous it becomes a thread connecting the chords, and that is its structural job in a trio, where the bass is the only member sustaining the pulse between the comping of the piano and the melody of the saxophone. The bass player is expected to know the tune and the harmony so that the line can pass through the right notes at the right moments, and a bass line that only hits roots leaves the ear with nothing to move to. The trap in the second option confuses the bass player's role with the pianist's, since both players need the full chord but they supply it differently, and the third option inverts the definition, since walking lines move by step and it is the leaps that a walking bass avoids.
questions.hint: Ask how many notes fall in a bar, whether any beat is unsounded, and what the line does between the chord tones.

questions.topic: How long a bar lasts under a walking bass
questions.learningObjective: convert a bar's beat count into seconds at a stated tempo
questions.stem: A walking bass line plays one note on every beat of a bar in common time, and the tempo is 132 quarter notes to the minute. How many seconds does one bar last?
questions.explanation: A bar of common time is four quarter notes, and one quarter note at 132 to the minute lasts sixty over one hundred and thirty-two of a second, so four beats take two hundred and forty over one hundred and thirty-two seconds. That is one point eight one eight, which rounds to one point eight two. The second route is to divide differently and check: one hundred and thirty-two goes into three hundred and sixty twice, so the tempo is a little under two beats a second, and four beats at slightly under half a second each come to a little under two seconds, which is consistent with one point eight two and not with two. The trap is two, which would be right at a tempo of one hundred and twenty, and the trap of half a second, which is the length of one beat and would be the answer to a question about the beat rather than the bar.
questions.hint: Multiply four beats by sixty divided by the tempo, and round to two decimal places.

questions.topic: What the bebop scale adds to a major scale
questions.learningObjective: state what note the bebop scale adds and what the added note is for
questions.stem: The g bebop major scale is written g4, a4, b4, c5, d5, e5, f-sharp5 and g-sharp5, so it has eight notes where a major scale has seven. Which note has been added and what is its function?

options.text: The g-sharp5 has been added between the f-sharp5 and the octave g, and it fills in the whole tone between those two notes so that a line of consecutive scale steps moves in whole tones and the strong beats of the line land on chord tones
The g-sharp5 has been added at the top of the scale, and it extends the scale by a whole tone so that lines built on it can reach a ninth above the tonic
options.misconception: describes the added note as an extension of the scale's range rather than a filling-in

options.text: The b4 has been added, because the major scale lacks a note between a and c and the bebop scale supplies it
options.misconception: names the wrong added note and misdescribes the gap

options.text: The g-sharp5 has been added between the f-sharp5 and the octave g, and its purpose is to make the scale unusable as a set of chord tones for a single chord
options.misconception: gives the added note the opposite of its real purpose

questions.explanation: The added note is the major seventh degree, g-sharp in this key, placed between the seventh degree and the octave, and the reason is entirely practical. In a major scale the top of the scale is a whole tone from the seventh degree to the octave, so a line moving in consecutive scale steps from the seventh degree to the octave jumps a whole tone and lands on the octave at a point where the beat is strong. A melody that is changing chords quickly wants the notes it lands on to be chord tones, and if the octave of the root arrives on a strong beat it may not be. Filling that whole tone with the g-sharp means the same consecutive-step line passes through the octave by semitone, and every note it reaches on a strong beat is by construction a member of the scale that the accompaniment of the moment is using. The trap in the fourth option states the opposite of the purpose, since the whole reason for the added note is that the scale should serve a single chord and its extensions well, and the trap in the second option mistakes a filling-in note for an extension of the range.
questions.hint: Locate the whole tone at the top of the scale and ask what a line of consecutive steps would do with it.

questions.topic: The step pattern of a bebop scale
questions.learningObjective: count the whole steps in a bebop scale's step pattern
questions.stem: Eight notes joined by seven steps make up the g bebop major scale, written g4, a4, b4, c5, d5, e5, f-sharp5 and g-sharp5. How many of those seven steps are whole steps?
questions.explanation: Walk up the scale and measure each step. From g4 to a4 is a whole step, a4 to b4 a whole step, b4 to c5 a half step, c5 to d5 a whole step, d5 to e5 a whole step, e5 to f-sharp5 a whole step and f-sharp5 to g-sharp5 a whole step. That is six whole steps and one half step, and six is the answer. The second route is to total the span: the scale runs from g4 to the g-sharp5 an octave above, which is thirteen semitones, and six whole steps is twelve semitones, leaving one semitone for the single half step, so the pattern must be six whole steps and one half. Six is also the count that distinguishes the bebop pattern from the major scale's, which has five whole steps and two half steps over the same seven intervals, the difference being that the added note turned the whole tone between the seventh degree and the octave into two whole steps.

questions.topic: How many chords a single chord scale serves
questions.learningObjective: state what a chord scale is and how many chords one scale can serve
questions.stem: A player improvises over a dominant seventh chord using a seven-note scale that contains the chord's root, third, fifth, seventh and three tensions. What is such a scale called, and how many chords can one instance of it serve?

options.text: It is a chord scale, and one instance can serve a single chord, because the tensions it contains are chosen for that chord and will clash with a different root or a different quality
It is a chord scale, and one instance can serve any chord of the same quality anywhere in the octave, because a chord scale contains every note those chords need
options.misconception: believes one scale covers every chord of a quality

options.text: It is a diatonic scale of the key, and one instance can serve all seven chords of that key, since a diatonic scale contains the notes of each of them
options.misconception: confuses a chord scale with a diatonic scale of the key

options.text: It is a mode, and one instance can serve the one chord whose root matches the mode, so a player needs one mode for every chord in the music
options.misconception: names a chord scale a mode and reduces it to a root match

questions.explanation: A chord scale is a scale built to fit one chord, and it is built by starting from the chord and adding the tensions that chord is characterised by, so that the three extra notes are the altered ninth, eleventh and thirteenth rather than anything chosen for the key. That is what makes it a chord scale rather than a mode, because a mode is derived from a scale and therefore serves whatever chords that scale supports, whereas a chord scale is derived from a chord and serves that chord. One instance serving one chord is the honest answer, and it is also the reason the device appears in improvisation: the player builds a scale in the first chorus and then alters individual notes in later choruses to follow the changes, which is a way of learning the harmony by ear. The trap in the second option is the confusion that a scale containing all the notes of a family of chords is therefore usable with all of them, which would make chord scales indistinguishable from modes.
questions.hint: Ask where the extra notes came from: from the chord being played, or from the key.

questions.topic: The normative resolution of a turnaround
questions.learningObjective: state the progression a jazz turnaround normally resolves to
questions.stem: At the end of a chorus in a blues in a, the band plays an e dominant seventh with a melody on b, and the next chorus begins on the a tonic triad. What is this two-chord move called and what is its normal resolution?

options.text: It is a turnaround, and its normative resolution is from the dominant seventh of the tonic to the tonic itself, so the melody's b rises a semitone to c and the whole chorus is re-entered
It is a turnaround, and its normative resolution is from the subdominant to the dominant, so the music must move away from the tonic rather than back to it
options.misconception: resolves a turnaround in the wrong direction entirely

options.text: It is a turnaround, and its normative resolution is from the tonic to the dominant, so the chorus begins on a dominant and works back to the tonic at its end
options.misconception: reverses which chord comes first in a turnaround

options.text: It is a turnaround, and its normative resolution is to the relative minor, so the chorus returns to the key a fourth above a minor rather than to a major
options.misconception: resolves a blues turnaround to the relative minor

questions.explanation: A turnaround is the pair of chords that closes a chorus and prepares the return, and its normative resolution is the dominant seventh of the key moving to the tonic, which in this case means an e7 resolving to an a major triad. The interval the root makes is a rising fourth, or equivalently a falling fifth, and the melodic reason the turnaround works is the same as the reason any dominant to tonic cadence works: the e7's third, g-sharp, and its seventh, d, are both pulling towards a and c, and the melody on the b sits a semitone below the c it will become. A turnaround is not, however, obliged to do this. The device is interesting precisely because it is a place where a player can substitute, so a blues chorus can end on the subdominant or on a chromatic chord and the audience accepts it. What is normative is the resolution the ear expects, not the chord that begins the figure.
questions.hint: Name the chord that begins the figure and ask which chord it most naturally resolves to.

questions.topic: How much of a mixolydian scale a dominant scale alters
questions.learningObjective: count the notes an altered dominant scale changes against mixolydian
questions.stem: A dominant altered scale on g is written g, a-flat, b-flat, c, d-flat, e-flat and f, and the g mixolydian scale is written g, a, b, c, d, e and f. How many of the altered scale's seven notes do not appear anywhere in the mixolydian scale?

The g, the c and the f appear in both, and the a-flat, the b-flat, the d-flat and the e-flat appear in neither, so four of the altered scale's notes are absent from mixolydian. The second route is to count the other way: mixolydian holds g, a, b, c, d, e and f, and of those the g, c and f survive in the altered scale, leaving the a, b, d and e replaced, which is four changes. Four is a large proportion, and it explains why the altered scale sounds as extreme as it does: it keeps the root, the fourth and the seventh of mixolydian and alters everything between them, so the flat ninth, the sharp ninth, the flat fifth and the flat thirteenth are all available at once. The trap is three, which counts the tensions of a dominant ninth chord and forgets that the natural third of mixolydian is one of the notes that has to be flattened to make the flat thirteenth available.

questions.stem: A blues in a ends a chorus with an e dominant seventh and the next chorus begins on the a tonic triad. The root of the dominant rises to the root of the tonic by a perfect fourth. Counting semitones, how wide is that rise?

Naming it is the check, since e to a spans the letter names e, f, g, a, which is a fourth, and a fourth of five semitones is a perfect fourth. questions.topic: The section form of a rhythm change
questions.learningObjective: state the section form of a rhythm change and how long each part is
questions.stem: A jazz standard is built from three sixteen-bar sections and one twenty-four-bar bridge, arranged so that the third section is the one that is different and the first section returns afterwards. What is the form called and what is the order?

options.text: It is a rhythm change in the order A, A, B, A, where each A is the same sixteen-bar theme and the B is the twenty-four-bar bridge placed at the bridge position of the form
It is a rhythm change in the order A, B, A, B, where the sixteen-bar theme and the twenty-four-bar bridge alternate evenly throughout the piece
options.misconception: alternates theme and bridge instead of placing the bridge at the bridge position

options.text: It is a thirty-two-bar form in the order A, A, B, A, and the twenty-four-bar section is counted as a second A because it returns to the tonic at its end
options.misconception: counts the bridge as one of the theme sections

options.text: It is a rondo in the order A, B, A, C, A, and the twenty-four-bar bridge is the contrasting episode of a rondo rather than a bridge
options.misconception: names a rondo and invents an extra section

questions.explanation: The form is the familiar four-section arrangement in which the same sixteen-bar theme is heard three times and the contrasting bridge is heard once, at the third position, so the order is A, A, B, A. The reason for that placement is tonal and formal together. The theme is built on a sequence of second-chord-to-dominant cadences in a single key, and hearing it a second time immediately confirms the key; the bridge then moves away from the key, often to the fourth degree or to a related key, and its return to the tonic at its end is what makes the third statement of the theme sound like a homecoming rather than a repetition. The thirty-two bars are the sum of three sixteens and one twenty-four, so the total matches the name of the form, and that arithmetic is the quickest way to check an arrangement. The first distractor puts the bridge at the second position, which removes the key confirmation before the departure, and the last names a rondo, whose refraining return is a different principle with a refrain rather than a theme.
questions.hint: Identify the one section that is different, and note that the theme is heard before and after it.

questions.stem: A jazz standard follows the common thirty-two-bar form made of three sixteen-bar theme sections and one twenty-four-bar bridge, in the order A, A, B, A. How many bars does the form contain in total?
questions.explanation: Three sixteen-bar sections come to forty-eight bars, and adding the twenty-four-bar bridge gives seventy-two. The second route is to total the thirty-two bars the form is named for and then add the eight the bridge is longer than a theme section by, since a bridge of twenty-four against a theme of sixteen is eight more, and thirty-two plus eight is forty. The third route is to add one section at a time: sixteen plus sixteen is thirty-two, thirty-two plus twenty-four is fifty-six, and fifty-six plus sixteen is seventy-two. The reason the total is worth knowing is that it names the form, since a form of thirty-two bars is the norm and any other total is a variation on it that a player has to learn separately. The trap is thirty-two, which is the name of the form rather than its arithmetic, and the trap of fifty-six, which omits the final return of the theme.
questions.hint: Add the three sixteen-bar sections, then add the twenty-four-bar bridge once.

questions.topic: Modal interchange and the chords it borrows
questions.learningObjective: state what modal interchange borrows and why the result sounds borrowed
questions.stem: A tune in c major suddenly uses the chord e-flat, g and b-flat, and then a chord of a, c and e-flat. Both chords come from a source the rest of the tune does not use. What is happening, and why is it recognisable as a borrowing?

options.text: The tune is borrowing from the parallel modes: the e-flat major triad is the flat submediant and the a minor triad is the flat supertonic, and they are recognisable because the raised fourth degree and the flattened third both pull away from the key the tune has established
The tune is borrowing from the relative minor, and the chords are recognisable because the minor key shares a key signature with the major and so the accidentals are the only clue
options.misconception: attributes the borrowing to the wrong mode

options.text: The tune is changing key for these two bars, and they are recognisable as a borrowing only because the accidentals have not yet been rewritten into the new key signature
options.misconception: mistakes a brief modal colour for a modulation

options.text: The tune is using chords from a neighbouring key a fourth above, and they are recognisable because a fourth away is the closest possible relationship between two keys
options.misconception: attributes the borrowing to a distant key relationship

questions.explanation: The chords come from the parallel modes rather than from a neighbouring key, and that is exactly what makes them sound like a colouring of the existing key rather than a departure from it. A flat submediant and a flat supertonic are the two most frequently borrowed chords in popular music, and the reason the ear hears them as borrowed is that both introduce notes which pull in a consistent direction. The e-flat in the submediant chord is a semitone above the tonic, and the e-flat in the supertonic chord makes that chord minor, so the borrowed notes are not random; they are the notes that give the borrowed modes their colour. Because both chords still have c in common with the key of the tune, and because the melody usually keeps to notes of c major over them, the tune never seems to have modulated. The trap in the second option is the interesting one, since the relative minor does share a key signature and so genuine modulation to it would need no accidentals at all, which is the opposite of what these chords require.
questions.hint: Ask which mode the borrowed notes come from, and check whether the melody stays inside the home key.

questions.topic: How many notes a borrowed chord adds
questions.learningObjective: count the notes a borrowed chord takes from outside the key
questions.stem: A tune in c major borrows the e-flat major triad, spelled e-flat, g and b-flat. The c major scale is c, d, e, f, g, a and b. How many of the borrowed chord's three notes lie outside the c major scale?
questions.explanation: Of the three notes, the g is in the c major scale and the e-flat and the b-flat are not, so two of the three are borrowed. The second route is to count what is left: three notes in the chord, one already belonging to the key, leaves two arriving from outside. The third route is to count the accidentals the chord needs, and a chord of e-flat, g and b-flat requires two flats that the c major key signature does not supply. Two is the number that makes the effect noticeable, because a borrowed chord that changed only one note would be a mere inflection, whereas one that changes two has a different colour altogether, and it is the presence of both lowered notes that gives the borrowed chord its sombre cast. The trap is one, which would count the flats as if the key signature supplied them, and the trap of three, which would mean none of the chord's notes belonged to the key.
questions.hint: Compare the three notes with the scale, and check the count against the accidentals the chord needs.

questions.topic: The distance to an altered thirteenth
questions.learningObjective: compute the semitone size of an altered thirteenth above a root
questions.stem: A dominant chord's thirteenth is a major sixth above the root. Altered, the thirteenth becomes a minor sixth instead. Counting semitones above the root c4, how high is the altered thirteenth?
questions.explanation: A minor sixth is eight semitones, so the altered thirteenth sits eight semitones above c4. The second route narrows the major sixth instead: a major sixth is nine semitones, and lowering the upper note by a semitone leaves eight. The third route names the note, since c4 numbered sixty plus eight is sixty-eight, and sixty-eight is the note a minor sixth above c4, which is a-flat4. Eight is worth contrasting with the flat ninth, which is one semitone, and with the thirteenth itself at nine semitones, since these three are the tensions a player chooses between when deciding how altered a dominant to make the chord sound. A flat thirteenth is the mildest of the alterations in this family, since it is only a semitone below the unaltered thirteenth, and it is the alteration that most often appears in a dominant ninth chord in a key where the thirteenth is already available diatonically.
questions.hint: Start from the major sixth and lower it by a semitone, or count up from the root.

questions.topic: The distance between a dominant and its tritone substitute
questions.learningObjective: compute the root distance to a tritone substitution
questions.stem: In c major a g7 chord, spelled g, b, d and f, is often replaced in performance by a d-flat7 chord, spelled d-flat, f, a-flat and c-flat. Counting semitones from g3 up to d-flat4, how far apart are the two roots?
questions.explanation: Up from g3, g-sharp is one, a two, a-sharp three, b four, c five and d-flat six, so the two roots are six semitones apart, a tritone. The second route measures the same distance downwards, since g3 down to d-flat3 is also six semitones, and a tritone is the same interval in either direction. The third route is the one that explains the device, and it is worth doing because it shows the substitution is not arbitrary: the g7 contains the tritone b and f, and the d-flat7 contains the tritone f and c-flat, and c-flat is the same sounding note as b, so the two chords share the two notes of their tritone exactly while the root and the fifth differ. Both resolve to the c major tonic, so the listener hears the same resolution and accepts the different root. The trap is four, which is a major third and is the distance to d-sharp, a chord that shares no notes at all with the g7.
questions.hint: Count up a semitone at a time, and then check which two notes the two chords have in common.

questions.topic: The aggregate of a row using every pitch class
questions.learningObjective: reduce the sum of a complete row's pitch classes modulo twelve
questions.stem: In twelve-tone writing a row uses each of the twelve pitch classes exactly once, numbered zero for c and rising by one semitone for each sharp. Adding the twelve numbers from zero to eleven gives a total of sixty-six. What is that total reduced modulo twelve?
questions.explanation: Reducing sixty-six modulo twelve means finding the remainder after the largest possible number of twelves, and twelve times five is sixty, so sixty-six less sixty is six. The second route is to add the numbers in pairs from the ends, so zero and eleven make eleven, one and ten make eleven, two and nine make eleven, three and eight make eleven, four and seven make eleven, and five and six make eleven, and that is six pairs of eleven, and six times eleven is sixty-six, which reduces the same way. Six is not a property of any particular row, since every row containing all twelve pitch classes has the same aggregate, and that is precisely the point: the sum is a check that the row is genuinely twelve-tone. A row that repeated a pitch class and omitted another would have a different total, and the discrepancy is what lets a composer or an analyst detect a slip.
questions.hint: Subtract the largest multiple of twelve that fits under the total, and check by pairing the numbers.

questions.topic: The aggregate of the second trichord of a row
questions.learningObjective: reduce the aggregate of one trichord of a partitioned row
questions.stem: A row begins with the pitch classes zero, four and seven, and then continues with nine, eleven and one, so the first six notes are partitioned into two trichords. The second trichord's three numbers add to twenty-one. What is that sum reduced modulo twelve?
questions.explanation: Twelve fits into twenty-one once, with a remainder of nine, so the reduced aggregate is nine. The second route adds the three numbers directly, which is nine plus eleven plus one, and nine plus eleven is twenty and twenty plus one is twenty-one, so the total is confirmed before the reduction. The third route is to reduce each number first and then add them, which is the form the rule usually takes: nine reduces to nine, eleven reduces to eleven, one reduces to one, and nine plus eleven plus one is again twenty-one, which reduces to nine. Reducing the members before adding is the same operation as reducing afterwards, and the reason composers compute a group's aggregate at all is to compare groups: two trichords of the same row may have the same aggregate or complementary ones, and that relationship is part of how the row's structure is analysed.
questions.hint: Subtract twelve from the total once, and check by adding the three numbers again.

questions.topic: The pitch classes a stated melody uses
questions.learningObjective: count the distinct pitch classes a stated melody uses
questions.stem: A melody is written c4 quarter note, e4 quarter note, f4 quarter note, a4 quarter note and c5 quarter note. Reduced to pitch classes, how many distinct pitch classes does the melody use?
questions.explanation: Reduce each note to a pitch class by discarding its octave: c4 and c5 both reduce to c, and e4, f4 and a4 each reduce to themselves, so the distinct classes are c, e, f and a, which is four. The second route is to count the five notes and subtract the one that is a repeat, since five notes with one duplication leaves four classes. The third route is to name the classes with numbers, counting c as zero, so the melody gives zero, four, five and nine, and there are four of them. Four is worth stating as a set-class observation, because a four-note set built from a major triad with one added note is one of the commonest shapes in tonal music, and counting the distinct classes rather than the notes is the first step of the analysis that identifies it. The trap is five, which counts the notes rather than the classes, and the trap of two, which would treat the c at the start and the c at the end as different.
questions.hint: Discard the octave numbers and count the distinct letter names, including the accidentals.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that inverts a motive
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that replaces each interval with its octave complement
questions.stem: Trace the rule invert(m), which returns the list of the motive's successive intervals with each one replaced by the distance from itself to twelve, and read the intervals of the motive c4 quarter, e4 quarter, g4 quarter, c5 half. What does the rule return?

options.text: Eight, nine and seven, since twelve less four is eight, twelve less three is nine and twelve less five is seven
Four, three and five, since the intervals are the motive's own and inversion reverses only their direction
options.misconception: treats inversion as leaving the interval sizes unchanged

options.text: Eight, nine and five, since only the intervals that are whole steps are replaced by their complements
options.misconception: inverts only the whole steps of the motive

options.text: Two, three and seven, since each interval is replaced by the distance that completes a perfect fifth with it
options.misconception: takes the complement to a perfect fifth rather than to an octave

questions.explanation: The rule has one job per interval, and the motive has three intervals because four notes make three gaps. The gaps are c4 up to e4, which is four semitones, e4 up to g4, which is three, and g4 up to c5, which is five. Each is replaced by the distance that completes an octave with it, and an octave is twelve semitones, so the results are twelve less four, twelve less three and twelve less five, which are eight, nine and seven. Checking against the interval names gives the same answer, since a major third inverts to a minor sixth of eight semitones, a minor third inverts to a major sixth of nine, and a perfect fourth inverts to a perfect fifth of seven. The trap in the second option is the commonest confusion about inversion, since a listener often hears the inverted figure as a paraphrase of the original and assumes nothing has changed. The third option inverts only part of the figure, and the fourth uses a perfect fifth as the reference when the rule is explicitly defined against an octave.
questions.hint: Measure the three gaps in the motive, then subtract each from twelve.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that counts a motive's statements
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that counts how many times a motive appears in a passage
questions.stem: Trace the rule matches(passage, motive), which returns the number of places in passage where motive appears in its exact form, at any pitch and in any octave, and the passage is c4, d4, e4, f4, g4, a4, b4, c5, c4, d4, e4, f4 with the motive c4, d4, e4. What does the rule return?

options.text: Two, because the figure occurs at the first three notes and again at notes nine to eleven, and there is no third occurrence in a passage of twelve notes
One, because the second statement is a repetition of the first and a repetition is not a fresh match of the motive
options.misconception: does not count a restatement of the motive as a match

options.text: Three, because the figure also overlaps itself at notes two to four, so an overlapping occurrence counts as well
options.misconception: counts overlapping occurrences of the motive

options.text: Four, because the rule counts the notes of the motive rather than the number of times the whole figure occurs
options.misconception: counts notes of the motive instead of statements of it

questions.explanation: The passage is an ascending scale of eight notes followed by the first four notes of the same scale again, so the figure c4, d4, e4 appears once in the first run and once in the second, which is two matches. The second route is to search for the motive from each position and reject the ones that run off the end: at note one the figure c4, d4, e4 is present, at note two the figure would be d4, e4, f4, which is not the motive, and the same rejection applies at every other position until note ten, where the passage has only three notes left and they are the motive. Two is the count a motivic analyst wants, because the question is how many times the composer asserted the figure, and a restatement in a new part of the passage is an assertion even though the notes are identical. The third trap comes from a rule that allowed a figure to begin in the middle of another statement of itself, and the fourth confuses the length of the motive with the number of its appearances.
questions.hint: Look for each starting position and ask whether the whole figure is present from there.
