questions.topic: Tracing a rule that builds a row matrix
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that reports the size of a twelve-tone matrix
questions.stem: Trace the rule matrix(row), which returns a grid in which each of the twelve rows is the row transposed up by one more semitone than the row above, together with the count(row) rule, which returns the number of distinct row forms the grid contains. Given a row of twelve pitch classes, what do the two rules report?

options.text: Twelve distinct row forms and one hundred and forty-four cells, since twelve rows each of twelve notes fill the grid and each successive fifth of the circle gives a new form
Six distinct row forms and seventy-two cells, since a row and its inversion are treated as one form and a tritone transposition repeats
options.misconception: halves the count by treating inversion as the same row

options.text: Twelve distinct row forms and twelve cells, since the rule counts the notes of one row rather than the cells of the whole grid
options.misconception: reports the length of one row as the size of the grid

options.text: Twenty-four distinct row forms and two hundred and eighty-eight cells, since the rule counts the rows and also the column forms separately
options.misconception: doubles the count by treating the columns as additional rows

questions.explanation: A matrix is built by stacking the twelve transpositions of a row, one for each of the twelve pitch classes, so there are twelve rows and each row has twelve notes, which is twelve times twelve or one hundred and forty-four cells. The number of distinct row forms is also twelve, since transposing a twelve-note row that uses every pitch class by a different number of semitones gives twelve different sequences with no repetitions among them. The second route is to note that a matrix is symmetric in a specific sense, since each column of the grid is one of the same twelve transpositions, and that is why the grid holds the row forms and the inversals of the row forms without needing a separate set. The trap in the second option comes from a confusion between the row and the inversion of the row, which are different sequences and are both present in the grid as separate forms. The fourth trap double-counts by treating the columns as though they added new material, when in fact they repeat what the rows already contain.
questions.hint: Count the rows from the number of pitch classes and the cells from rows times notes.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that finds a set's prime form
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that reports the prime form of a pitch-class set
questions.stem: Trace the rule prime(s), which takes a set s, transposes it so that its lowest note becomes zero, and also does the same to the inversion of s, then returns whichever of the two packs the notes most tightly against zero. Applied to the set zero, one, two and three, what does the rule return and why?

options.text: Zero, one, two and three, because the set is already packed from zero and its span of three semitones is the tightest of any transposition or inversion available
One, two, three and four, because the rule always transposes upwards to avoid leaving a zero in the set
options.misconception: assumes the rule avoids a zero in the set

options.text: Zero, nine, ten and eleven, because the inversion of the set is more compact than the set itself
options.misconception: believes the inversion packs more tightly than the original

options.text: Zero, two, four and six, because packing a set means redistributing it as evenly spaced notes
options.misconception: substitutes a regularly spaced set for the one given

questions.explanation: Packing means moving every note down by the same amount so that the lowest sits at zero, and the span is the distance from the lowest note to the highest. The set zero, one, two and three is already packed, and its span is three semitones, which is the smallest any transposition can produce because moving the set only slides it. The inversion is the set zero, eleven, ten and nine, which is the same set read from the other direction, and its span is nine semitones, so it is far less compact and the rule keeps the original. The second route is to count the gaps: the set zero, one, two, three has three gaps of one semitone each, and the inverted version zero, nine, ten, eleven has three gaps of one, one and one measured downwards, but its span from zero to eleven is eleven semitones, so the span comparison favours the original. Zero is also the number the definition requires, since a packed set is always measured from zero, which is what makes a prime form comparable between different transpositions of the same set.
questions.hint: Pack the set from zero, invert it, pack that from zero, and compare the two spans.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that audits parallel perfect intervals
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that reports every pair of parts moving in parallel perfect intervals
questions.stem: Trace the rule audit(v1, v2), which compares the interval between every pair of parts in two chords and returns the name of any pair whose interval is a perfect fifth or an octave in both chords, with the pairs listed as soprano-alto, soprano-tenor, soprano-bass, alto-tenor, alto-bass and tenor-bass. Applied to c major, the first chord voiced g4, c4, e3 and c3 moving to a dominant voiced d4, g3, b2 and g2, what does the rule return?

options.text: Three pairs, soprano and alto, soprano and bass, and alto and bass, since the soprano and alto keep a fifth, the outer voices keep a twelfth and the alto and bass keep an octave
One pair, soprano and alto, since the fifth between them is the only perfect interval that both chords share
options.misconception: reports only the first of the three faults it finds

options.text: No pairs, since both chords are consonant on their own and two consonant chords cannot make a fault between them
options.misconception: believes a fault requires one of the chords to be dissonant

options.text: Six pairs, since every part moves down the same interval and so every pair of parts must be in parallel
options.misconception: assumes a common motion interval makes every pair parallel

questions.explanation: The rule compares all six pairs, and three of them match. The soprano and alto keep a perfect fifth, since g4 down to c4 is seven semitones and d4 down to g3 is seven as well. The soprano and bass keep the same interval, g4 above c3 being nineteen semitones and d4 above g2 being nineteen, and nineteen is an octave plus a fifth, so this is also a parallel fifth in compound form. The alto and bass keep an octave, since c4 above c3 is twelve and g3 above g2 is twelve. The remaining three pairs, soprano and tenor, alto and tenor, and tenor and bass, move between intervals of different sizes, so the rule rejects them. This is the pattern that makes an audit worth running rather than eyeballing, because the three faults in this progression are of three different kinds and only the first is the one a reader would notice. The trap in the fourth option is the arithmetic error of assuming that because all four parts move down the same interval, every pair must be at fault, when in fact only the pairs that were already a perfect fifth or an octave stay that way.
questions.hint: Measure all six pairs in both chords and list the ones whose interval is unchanged and perfect.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that checks a chord's doubling
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that reports a doubled note and whether the doubling is faulty
questions.stem: Trace the rules doubled(chord, voicing), which returns the note of chord that appears twice in voicing, and warned(chord), which returns true when the doubled note is the root of a diminished triad. Applied to the leading-tone diminished triad of c major, voiced as d3, f3, b3 and b4, what do the two rules return?

options.text: The doubled note is b, and the warning is true, because b is the root of a diminished triad and a first-inversion diminished triad should double its third, d
The doubled note is d, and the warning is false, because d is already the bass note and a bass note is never the doubled one
options.misconception: assumes the bass note cannot also be doubled

options.text: The doubled note is b, and the warning is false, because doubling the root of a chord is acceptable in every quality of chord
options.misconception: believes a doubled root is always safe

options.text: The doubled note is f, and the warning is true, because f is the diminished seventh of the chord and so cannot be doubled
options.misconception: misidentifies which note of the chord appears twice

questions.explanation: The four notes of the leading-tone diminished triad of c major are b, d and f, and the voicing sounds d3, f3, b3 and b4, so the b appears twice and every other note once. The chord is a triad with a diminished quality, which means it is built from two stacked minor thirds, and its root is the lowest of those thirds, which is b. The warning therefore fires, because doubling the root of a diminished triad is the fault the rule is looking for. The reason is tonal: in this chord the b is the leading tone, a note that has to rise a semitone to the tonic, and a doubled leading tone means one of the two copies has nowhere to go and must stay put, leaving a note a semitone below the tonic sounding after the tonic has arrived. A first-inversion diminished triad is normally written with its third doubled for exactly this reason, and here the third is d, which is the bass. The trap in the fourth option confuses the seventh of the chord with its root, and the trap in the second option misreads the role of the bass.
questions.hint: Count how many times each note of the chord sounds, then ask which chord member the bass note is.

questions.topic: Finding a motive's statements in a stated passage
questions.learningObjective: locate a stated motive's statements in a stated passage
questions.stem: A passage in c major is given note by note. Bar one is g4 quarter, b4 quarter, c5 half. Bar two is e4 half, then g4, b4 and c5 in quarters. Bar three is c4, e4, g4 and b4 in half notes, then bar four is g4, b4, c5 and e5, the last two as half notes. Bar five begins d4, f4, e4 and c4 in quarters. In how many of these five bars does the opening figure appear, and in which bars?

options.text: Four bars, which are bars one, two, three and four, and the fifth bar inverts the figure so that it no longer appears in its original form
Five bars, because the figure is stated in every bar and the fifth bar merely moves it down a third
options.misconception: misses that the fifth bar inverts rather than transposes the figure

options.text: Three bars, which are bars one, two and three, and bars four and five both alter the figure too much to count
options.misconception: misses the transposition in bar four

options.text: Two bars, which are bars one and two, and the later bars are sequence repetitions rather than statements of the motive
options.misconception: refuses to count a statement at a different pitch

questions.explanation: The figure is g4, b4, c5, a major third followed by a minor second. Bar one states it at the original pitch, bar two states it an octave lower, bar three states it with the same interval pattern at a lower start, bar four states it an octave above the original, and bar five is d4, f4, e4, c4, which is the same interval pattern read downwards, so it is an inversion rather than a statement. Four bars is the count a motivic analysis reports, and the important methodological point is that a statement at a different pitch is still a statement. The trap in the second option is treating the fifth bar as a transposition when the direction of every interval has reversed, and the trap in the third option is over-strictness, since a motive transposed up an octave is more recognisable, not less. The fourth trap mistakes sequence for motivic analysis, since a motive is precisely what a sequence repeats.
questions.hint: Write out the interval pattern of the opening figure and check it in each bar, allowing for transposition but not for inversion.

questions.topic: Analysing the form of a stated section
questions.learningObjective: identify the sections of a stated movement and their cadences
questions.stem: A movement's first sixteen bars are described bar by bar. Bars one to four are in c major and end on a c major triad with the melody on e. Bars five to eight move to f major and back to c major. Bars nine to twelve move to g7 and then to c major. Bars thirteen to sixteen leave c major, arrive at a minor, and end on a root-position a minor triad with the melody on e. How do these sixteen bars divide, and what is the plan?

options.text: Four phrases of four bars, which form a period, because the first three phrases end on the tonic and the fourth ends on the submediant, and the fourth phrase is then the answer that withholds the close
Two phrases of eight bars, which form a sentence, because the first eight bars present the melody and the second eight bars continue it before the close
options.misconception: reads the material as one long sentence rather than as two cadential units

options.text: One sixteen-bar period, because a period's two phrases need not be of equal length so long as the harmonic plan is parallel
options.misconception: requires a period's two phrases to be of equal length

options.text: Four phrases forming a double period, because four phrases of equal length always constitute a double period rather than a single one
options.misconception: counts phrases without testing how they cadence

questions.explanation: The cadences are what decide this, and reading them in order gives a tonic arrival at bar four, another at bar eight, another at bar twelve and a submediant arrival at bar sixteen. So the phrases are four bars each, the first three end on the tonic and the fourth ends on the submediant, and a submediant arrival is a close that withholds the tonic, so the listener hears the section as answered and then left standing on a chord that is not home. That is what makes the sixteen bars one period rather than two, because a period's second half is the half that closes, and here the closing half is the one that refuses the tonic. A sentence would behave differently, since its defining feature is that the first half does not cadence at all and the arrival is postponed to the very end, whereas here there is a clear tonic arrival at bar four. The third trap invents a rule about unequal phrase lengths, and the fourth trap counts phrases without asking how they cadence, which is the only thing that distinguishes a double period from a single one.
questions.hint: Find the cadential chord at the end of each phrase and see which tonic or non-tonic each one arrives on.

questions.topic: Reading a table of dominant extensions and their tensions
questions.learningObjective: match dominant extensions and altered chords to the tensions they add
questions.stem: A table gives four chords built on c, each with a c in the bass. Row 1 has e, g and b-flat, giving a minor ninth above the bass. Row 2 has e, g, b-flat and b, giving a minor ninth and a major seventh. Row 3 has e-flat, g, b-flat and a, giving a flat fifth, a flat seventh, a flat ninth and a thirteenth. Row 4 has e, g, b, d and a, giving a third, a seventh, a ninth and a thirteenth. Which row is the altered dominant, and which two rows differ only in the quality of their seventh?

options.text: Row 3 is the altered dominant, and rows 1 and 2 differ only in that row 1's seventh is flat while row 2's seventh is natural
Row 4 is the altered dominant, and rows 2 and 3 differ only in that row 2's third is natural while row 3's third is flat
options.misconception: misses the flattened fifth and seventh that make row 3 altered

options.text: Row 1 is the altered dominant, and rows 3 and 4 differ only in that row 3 has a flat third while row 4 has a natural third
options.misconception: calls a plain minor ninth chord the altered dominant

options.text: Row 2 is the altered dominant, and rows 1 and 4 differ only in the number of notes, since one has four and the other five
options.misconception: treats a difference in chord size as the distinction between the rows

questions.explanation: An altered dominant is a dominant chord in which one or more of its notes are chromatically altered, and row 3 is the only one that alters the fifth and the seventh as well as adding tensions: the flat fifth and the flat seventh are the alterations that give the row its name, and a chord with a natural fifth and a major seventh is not altered at all. Rows 1 and 2 are the clearest pair in the table because they are otherwise identical, both being a triad on c with a minor ninth, and they differ in exactly one note, the seventh, which is flat in row 1 and natural in row 2. That single note is what decides whether the chord reads as a minor ninth chord with a major seventh, which sounds unresolved, or as a dominant, which does not. The traps here are all about counting alterations rather than locating them, and the last one is the reminder that adding a note is extension while changing a note is alteration.
questions.hint: Ask which row changes a note of a plain dominant seventh, rather than only adding notes to it.

questions.topic: Reading a table of twelve-tone rows
questions.learningObjective: identify transpositions from a table of rows
questions.stem: A table lists four rows of pitch-class numbers. Row A is zero, two, four, five, seven, nine, eleven, one, three, six, eight, ten. Row B is one, three, five, six, eight, ten, zero, two, four, seven, nine, eleven. Row C is zero, four, seven, eleven, two, five, nine, one, four, eight, eleven, three. Row D is eleven, one, three, four, six, eight, ten, zero, two, five, seven, nine. Which rows are transpositions of row A, and which row fails to use all twelve pitch classes?

options.text: Rows B and D are transpositions of row A, and row C is the one that fails, since it repeats zero and four and never uses the pitch class ten
Rows B and C are transpositions of row A, and row D is the one that fails, since it has no accidentals at all
options.misconception: misses the repeated pitch class in row C

options.text: Only row B is a transposition of row A, and row C is the one that fails, since its second half is a different row altogether
options.misconception: misses that row D is also a transposition

options.text: All four rows are transpositions of row A, and none fails, since every row uses the same twelve notes in a different order
options.misconception: assumes a transposition can repeat a pitch class

questions.explanation: A transposition adds the same number to every note of the row and then reduces each result modulo twelve, so the test is whether the intervals between successive notes are unchanged. Row B is row A with one added to every note, and the reduction is visible in the seventh position, where row A's eleven becomes zero. Row D is row A with one subtracted from every note, and the reduction is visible at the start, where row A's zero becomes eleven, so both are transpositions. Row C is not a transposition, because the gaps between its successive notes differ from row A's, and it also fails the twelve-tone requirement: it uses zero twice and four twice and never uses ten, so it is not a row at all but a twelve-note sequence. The traps are worth noting because each corresponds to a real temptation, and the last one is the important one, since a transposition of a genuine row cannot repeat a pitch class, so a row that does is not a transposition of anything.
questions.hint: Add one to every note of row A and reduce modulo twelve, and check each row for repeated numbers.

questions.topic: A structural claim the stated material contradicts
questions.learningObjective: reject a formal claim that the stated material cannot support
questions.stem: A commentary claims that a movement's opening is a ritornello, on the grounds that the same instrumental passage recurs four times between the soloist's entries and that each recurrence is in a different key. The opening passage is described as being twenty-four bars long for full orchestra with no solo part, and the soloist's first entry comes after the first statement has finished. Does the stated material support the claim?

options.text: Yes, because a ritornello is a self-contained orchestral passage that returns between solo entries, and the different key at each recurrence is part of how a ritornello is defined
No, because a ritornello returns at the same pitch throughout and the use of different keys makes the passage a theme and variations instead
options.misconception: assumes a ritornello cannot change key between returns

options.text: No, because the passage is twenty-four bars long, and a ritornello is always short enough to be stated in eight bars
options.misconception: judges a ritornello by its length alone

options.text: No, because the soloist enters only once, and a ritornello requires several solo entries to frame at all
options.misconception: demands a number of solo entries the passage does not show

questions.explanation: The claim holds, and every part of it is one of the conditions a ritornello imposes. The passage is self-contained, being twenty-four bars for full orchestra with no soloist, which is what lets it be heard as a unit rather than as accompaniment. It returns, and it returns between solo entries, which is the framing function. And it returns in a different key each time, which is not a departure from the form but part of it, since the change of key is how the return registers as a new stage of the movement's journey and how the soloist's excursions are measured. The second trap is the one that catches people who know the device only in a single-key version, and the third trap is a matter of proportion rather than definition, since ritornelli of twenty bars and longer are entirely ordinary and a length limit is not part of the concept. The fourth trap demands evidence the passage does not supply, since the commentary describes the first solo entry and the claim concerns the pattern of returns.
questions.hint: Check the three conditions a ritornello must meet: self-contained, returning, and framing solo entries.

questions.topic: Finding a fault in a stated four-part progression
questions.learningObjective: identify the faulty voice pair in a stated four-part progression
questions.stem: A four-part progression in c major is given as two chords. The first has b3 in the soprano, g3 in the alto, d3 in the tenor and b2 in the bass. The second has c4 in the soprano, g3 in the alto, e3 in the tenor and c3 in the bass. Which pair of parts moves in parallel perfect intervals, and why is that pair the only one?

options.text: The soprano and the bass, because they move from an octave apart to an octave apart, while the other pairs change size, with the alto staying put and no other pair keeping a perfect interval
The alto and the tenor, because they are the two middle parts and the middle parts are where faults usually occur
options.misconception: assumes faults occur in the middle parts by default

options.text: No pair, because the second chord is a complete tonic triad in root position and a complete chord cannot contain a fault
options.misconception: believes a complete chord rules out a voice-leading fault

options.text: All four parts, because every part rises by the same small interval and equal motion in all parts is itself the fault
options.misconception: treats similar motion as a fault regardless of the intervals

questions.explanation: Measure every pair in both chords. The soprano and bass are an octave apart in the first chord, since b3 and b2 are the same note an octave apart, and an octave apart in the second, since c4 and c3 are, so the octave is preserved and that pair moves in parallel octaves. The soprano and alto change size, since b3 above g3 is five semitones and c4 above g3 is seven, and the alto stays put, so there is no parallel interval. The soprano and tenor change from a sixth to an octave, and the alto and tenor from a third to a fourth, so neither of those is preserved either. The alto's common tone is what saves the other three pairs, and a reader who checks only the outer voices will conclude the same thing here, whereas a reader who checks nothing will guess. The trap in the third option confuses the completeness of a chord with the legality of the connection between two chords, which are entirely separate matters.
questions.hint: Write out the six pairs in both chords and look for the one whose interval is the same perfect interval twice.

questions.topic: A canon that doubles the time of every entry
questions.learningObjective: explain how a canon by augmentation works and what it makes of the tune
questions.stem: Two voices perform the same melody of four bars, the second voice entering two bars after the first and singing every note at twice its written value. Explain how the canon works, and what the augmentation does to the tune as it is heard.

answer.exemplar: A canon by augmentation is a canon in which the follower sings the same melody as the leader but at a slower rate, and everything about its effect follows from that single change. Here the leader sings four bars of music at the written tempo and the follower enters two bars later with every note value doubled, so the follower takes eight bars to sing what the leader took four. The two voices are therefore out of step with each other in a very specific way. The follower is permanently behind, and the amount of the lag is not constant in musical terms even though the entry distance is: because the follower's values are twice as long, the two versions of any one note do not coincide, they are stretched apart, and the tune is heard simultaneously at two different tempos. That is the source of the music's character. A plain canon superimposes one version of a tune on another at the same speed, which produces a texture that is rhythmically unified and harmonically interesting, and a canon by augmentation replaces that unity with a long, breathing discrepancy. The follower is always behind and therefore never in phase, so the melody cannot be followed vertically, and the listener hears the tune as a whole drifting against itself. This is why the device appears in slow music, where the long values suit the character of the instruments, and why it is often combined with a change of octave, since a follower an octave lower keeps the two lines audibly distinct when they are at different tempos. The composer also gains a harmonic problem to solve, because the interval between the two versions of the same note changes constantly as the leader moves through the tune, and those intervals have to be made consonant by the harmony rather than by the melody. The wrong belief to avoid is that augmentation is a rhythmic device for making a canon easier to sing. Its effect is the opposite of that, since the point is precisely that the two lines cannot be sung as a single rhythm.

questions.explanation: A canon by augmentation has the follower sing the same melody in double-length values, so the two versions of the tune are permanently out of phase and the lag is stretched rather than aligned. The effect is a long breathing discrepancy between the lines rather than rhythmic unity, which is why the device suits slow music and is often combined with an octave displacement. The trap is treating augmentation as a way of simplifying a canon, when its whole point is that the lines cannot be followed as one rhythm.
questions.hint: Ask how long the first voice has sung when the second begins, and what happens to the note values in between.

questions.topic: When a quotation is fair to the work it comes from
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a musical quotation defensible
questions.stem: A movement quotes eight bars from a work written a century earlier, places the quotation inside a completely different texture and in a different key, and alters its rhythm so that the notes no longer fall where the original placed them. Explain what the composer has done and what makes the borrowing defensible rather than merely convenient.

answer.exemplar: The composer has made an allusion, and the question of whether it is defensible turns on how a listener is meant to recognise it. Eight bars of melody quoted note for note in a new key and a new rhythm, with no acknowledgement, is not an allusion but a lift: it takes the most identifiable thing in the older work, the material a listener is most likely to recognise, and reproduces it without the context that would tell a listener what is being referred to. A defensible quotation does the opposite. It changes enough that the passage is genuinely the new composer's, and it changes the pitch level and the accompaniment so that the quoted material is heard as a shape rather than as a tune, and it places the quotation at a point where the older work's character is relevant, so that the resemblance carries meaning rather than merely existing. The key change and the rhythmic alteration in this example are both on the right side of that line. Transposing a quotation keeps its melodic intervals, so the contour and the phrase structure survive, which is what allows recognition, while moving it away from the original key stops the ear from placing it in the old work. Altering the rhythm has a similar effect, because rhythm is a strong identifier of a melody and changing it reduces the number of clues a listener has. What makes the borrowing defensible is therefore not that it is unrecognisable but that it is recognisable in the right way: a listener should hear a familiar shape acquire a new meaning, and should be able to say afterwards what the reference was for. If the quotation functions as a joke, the older material must be present enough for the joke to work, and if it functions as an argument, the resemblance must be exact enough that the argument has a target. The wrong belief to avoid is that any transformation of a borrowed passage makes it the new composer's own. Transforming a quotation is a way of quoting, and the composer who alters it is still using the older composer's invention, which is why the amount of transformation and the reason for it are the two things that have to be judged.

questions.explanation: The composer has made an allusion by transposing and re-rhythming the quoted bars, which keeps the melodic shape recognisable while moving the music away from the older work's key and character. Defensibility depends on recognition in the right way rather than on unrecognisability, so the reference has to carry meaning. The trap is that any transformation makes a borrowing the new composer's own, when a transformed quotation is still a quotation.
questions.hint: Ask how a listener identifies the quotation at all, and what the composer had to change to make it his own.

questions.topic: What a tribute borrows and what it leaves behind
questions.learningObjective: explain what a tribute reproduces and what a tribute must change
questions.stem: A movement is described in print as a tribute to an earlier composer's manner. It reproduces that composer's characteristic phrase lengths and the shape of the harmony, but its melody, its orchestration and its tempo are entirely the new composer's own. Explain what the tribute has borrowed and why these choices matter.

answer.exemplar: A tribute borrows the composable habits of an earlier writer rather than that writer's music, and the distinction between the two is the whole subject. What is habit and what is music is partly a matter of degree, but it is a useful degree to state. Phrase length is habit: a composer who consistently writes four-bar phrases and answers them with four-bar phrases has a way of organising time that a listener can recognise without hearing a single note of the melody. The shape of the harmony is close to habit for the same reason, since a pattern of moving towards a dominant and away from it again is a structural decision that survives a change of notes. Melody is much closer to music, because a melody is the part of a work that a listener remembers and identifies most specifically, and it is also the part protected most tightly by custom and by law. Orchestration and tempo sit in between, being recognisably a composer's property but less protected than the notes themselves. This is why the tribute described here takes the first two and leaves the other three, and the choice is a coherent one rather than a convenient one. By borrowing phrase length and harmonic shape, the composer is showing a listener how the older music was put together, which is a claim about method; by replacing melody, orchestration and tempo, the composer is making a claim about himself. A listener who hears the resemblance is therefore being given something real, namely a demonstration that the same structural habits can carry completely different notes. The movement's interest lies in the difference between what is preserved and what is not, since the borrowed framework makes the new content more audible, in the way that repeating a word makes the change of the next word easier to hear. The wrong belief to avoid is that a tribute must be vague in order to be respectful. The reverse is closer to the truth: a tribute that preserves nothing cannot be recognised as a tribute at all, and a tribute that preserves everything is not a tribute but a copy. The composer has to make the resemblance exact enough to be heard and different enough to be worth hearing, and the two requirements pull against each other, which is why the choices in a tribute are worth analysing rather than simply admiring.

questions.explanation: A tribute borrows structural habits such as phrase length and harmonic shape, which show method without reproducing the music, and replaces melody, orchestration and tempo, which are the most specifically identifying and most heavily protected. The resemblance has to be exact enough to be heard and different enough to be worth hearing, so the borrowed framework is what makes the new content audible. The trap is that a respectful tribute should be vague, when precision of reference is what makes it a tribute at all.
questions.hint: Ask which features of the older music are structural and which are surface, and what a listener is being shown.

questions.topic: The condition a direct fifth obeys and a leading tone that does not
questions.learningObjective: explain when an outer-voice fifth is permitted and how a leading tone may not be directed
questions.stem: In g major, a progression moves from a dominant triad with d3 in the bass and a3 in the soprano to a tonic triad with g3 in the bass and d4 in the soprano. The soprano leaps a fourth and the outer voices arrive at a perfect fifth. In a second passage, the soprano holds the leading tone of c major, b4, over the dominant, and instead of rising to c5 it rises to d5. Explain what makes the first passage acceptable and the second a fault.

answer.exemplar: The two passages fail and succeed for reasons that need to be separated, because they are two different faults. A direct fifth, sometimes called a hidden fifth, is the name for the situation in which the outer voices of a chord move in the same direction and arrive at a perfect fifth. On its own this is not a fault; the danger is that two parts arriving at a perfect fifth in similar motion can be heard momentarily as a single line, and the resulting doubling of the root destroys the interval's stability. The rule therefore turns on how the upper voice travelled. In the first passage the soprano moves from a3 to d4, which is a leap of a fourth, and that is exactly the case the rule forbids. So the first passage as described is a fault and not an acceptable one, and the passage that the rule permits is the one in which the upper voice moves by step, a second, so that the ear is given a moving line to follow and does not have to reconcile two voices arriving together. The exception exists because a step in the upper voice proves that the two parts are not moving as one, and the fifth is then reached from a position where the voices are demonstrably independent. The second passage is a fault of a different kind and one that no exception rescues. The leading tone of c major is b, and its function is to rise a semitone to the tonic. Rising instead to d5 is a leap of a minor third, and it does two kinds of damage at once. It leaves the leading tone unresolved, so the dominant never arrives at the tonic, and it moves the soprano onto the third of the tonic chord, where it sits against the direction the ear was promised by the previous chord. A leading tone that goes up must go up by a semitone, and a leading tone that goes down does so to the fifth of the tonic, which is a different and much rarer repair. The wrong belief to avoid is that the two faults are of the same kind. A direct fifth is about the relationship between two voices and can be permitted under a stated condition, whereas a misdirected leading tone is about a single note failing to do the one thing it exists to do, and no amount of correct handling elsewhere repairs it.

questions.explanation: A direct fifth is a fault when the upper voice leaps and is permitted when it moves by step, because a step proves the two outer voices are independent; the first passage leaps a fourth, so it is the faulted case. The second passage is a different kind of error: a leading tone that rises by a minor third to the tonic's third has failed the one function it exists to perform, and no exception permits it. The trap is treating the two as one fault when the first is about the relationship between two voices and the second about a single unresolved note.
questions.hint: Ask how the upper voice reached the fifth in the first passage, and what the leading tone was supposed to do in the second.

questions.topic: Ranking row forms by their transposition
questions.learningObjective: rank transposed row forms by their distance from the original
questions.stem: A composer has written four forms of one twelve-tone row. Form one is the original row. Form two is the row transposed up one semitone. Form three is the row transposed up three semitones. Form four is the row transposed up six semitones. Put the four forms in order from the one closest in pitch to the original to the one furthest away.

options.text: The original row, then the row up one semitone, then the row up three semitones, then the row up six semitones, since zero, one, three and six increase in that order
The original row, then the row up three semitones, then the row up one semitone, then the row up six semitones, since three is closer to six than one is
options.misconception: judges closeness by position within the list rather than by the size of the interval

options.text: The row up one semitone, then the original row, then the row up three semitones, then the row up six semitones, since the original sounds above its first transposition
options.misconception: orders the original after its own nearest transposition

options.text: The row up six semitones, then the row up three semitones, then the row up one semitone, then the original row, since the largest transposition is heard first
options.misconception: ranks the forms from furthest to nearest

questions.explanation: The criterion is a single number for each form, namely how many semitones it was transposed by, and the four numbers are zero, one, three and six. Sorting those gives zero, one, three, six, which is the original row first and the tritone transposition last. The reason the answer is worth stating in this form is that the tritone is the interesting one, because a transposition of six semitones is neither near nor far by any harmonic measure: it is the interval at which two transpositions of the same row sound least alike, since a listener cannot hear six semitones as a step or as a fifth. The distractors each fail in a different way. The second mistakes the order of the numbers in the sentence for their order by size, which is the commonest reading error in a ranking question. The third puts the original after its nearest transposition, on the false ground that the original was written later and so sounds higher, and the fourth reverses the criterion entirely, which is a ranking task answered with the opposite order.
questions.hint: Write the four transposition sizes as numbers and sort them, remembering that the original is zero.

questions.topic: Ranking the voices of a canon by how much they have played
questions.learningObjective: rank the voices of a canon by their progress when the last voice enters
questions.stem: A round for four voices has an eight-bar tune, and the voices enter at bars one, three, five and seven in that order, being voice one, voice two, voice three and voice four. At the moment the last voice begins, the earlier bars of the tune are complete. Put the four voices in order from fewest completed bars of the tune to most completed.

options.text: Voice four, then voice three, then voice two, then voice one, since by bar seven they have completed zero, two, four and six bars of the tune respectively
Voice one, then voice two, then voice three, then voice four, since the voice that starts first has the most of the tune behind it at any moment
options.misconception: ranks the voices from most complete to least complete

options.text: Voice two, then voice one, then voice four, then voice three, since the two-bar gap makes the second voice twice as far along as the first
options.misconception: treats the entry gap as a progress multiplier

options.text: Voice three, then voice two, then voice four, then voice one, since the third voice completes a whole number of two-bar units and the others do not
options.misconception: prefers the voice whose completed bars divide evenly

questions.explanation: The moment in question is the entry of the last voice, which is bar seven, and at that point bars one to six are complete for anybody who started at bar one. Voice one entered at bar one and has therefore completed six bars. Voice two entered at bar three and has completed four, since bars one and two passed before it began. Voice three entered at bar five and has completed two. Voice four has just begun and has completed none. The four numbers are zero, two, four and six, and sorting them from smallest to largest puts the last voice first. The arithmetic is simpler than it looks because the entries are evenly spaced, so the completed counts come out as an arithmetic sequence, and the second route is to note that each voice is exactly two bars behind the one before it, which is a single fact doing all the work. The first distractor ranks the voices the other way round, which is the commonest slip because a reader thinks of the first voice as the important one. The third treats the entry gap as though it multiplied the progress, when in fact the earlier voice has the larger total simply because it began earlier.
questions.hint: At the last entry, count how many bars have finished for each voice, and remember each voice began two bars after the one before.
